title.narrative: Support to Government`s Lean Season Response 2022/2023

description.narrative:
Approximately 3.8 million in acute food insecurity and in need of food assistance for 2-5 months. The deterioration in food security is attributed to climate-related shocks, high staple food prices and economic decline. The deterioration in food security is attributed to climate-related shocks, high staple food prices and economic decline. The climate-related shocks were characterised by late onset and early cessation of rainfall coupled with localised dry spells and flooding induced by tropical storms. This resulted in low crop production. The maize prices are generally higher than the past five-year average. Furthermore, a 25 percent devaluation of the Malawi Kwacha contributed to inflation. This, coupled with impact of the Ukraine crisis that has disrupted the global supply chain, has exerted further pressure on prices of essential items including fertilizers, fuel and wheat products. A high proportion of the population will start depleting their food stocks from October 2022; this may be exacerbated by reduced casual labour opportunities and negative coping strategies for households. The food gap analysis varies from district to district and cities, but assistance is required as early as November 2022 for periods of three to five months.
The expected per household transfer value is estimated at USD 24 (MWK 25,000)/month
The Malawi vulnerability assessment committee (MVAC) integrated food security phase classification (IPC) analysis for the 2022/2023 lean season shows that 3.8 million people in Malawi (20 percent of the population) are expected to face high levels of acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3), between October 2022 and March 2023. This is substantially higher than the 1.6 million in the 2021/2022 lean season. The number of districts classified in crisis (IPC Phase 3) is has increased from six to 21, including the four cities.
